newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian artist paints herself as Aboriginal man.
newsitem.headline: Australian artist paints herself as Aboriginal man.

text.p: Indigenous Australians were outraged on Friday to learn that an Aboriginal artist who won acclaim for his vibrant paintings and photographs was the invention of a rich and elderly white woman.
Aboriginal art experts accused Elizabeth Durack, the 81-year-old scion of a famous outback pioneer family, of stealing indigenous culture through her deception.
"It's the last thing left that you could possibly take away other than the rest of our lives or shoot us all," Aboriginal art curator John Mundine told Reuters.
"It seems to be some sort of personal whim, but basically she is white and can never be black," said Mundine, a senior curator at Sydney's Museum of Contemporary Art.

Durack, a cattle queen from the remote north-west Kimberley region, has admitted working under the name and background of a character she created, an Aboriginal farm worker aged in his 50s whom she named Eddie Burrup.

It is the second fake identity scandal to rock Australia's arts community in less than two years. In 1995, author Helen Darville admitted making up her family history to match an award-winning book, written under the name Helen Demidenko, about the slaughter of Ukrainian Jews during World War Two.
As Burrup, Durack's critically-praised works include paintings, photographs and even an autobiography.
Three works are part of a national touring exhibition of Aboriginal art and another painting has been entered for a national Aboriginal art award.
Durack, a well-known painter in her own right, confessed to her deception in a local arts magazine but refused to explain herself to journalists.
A friend and art historian, Robert Smith, defended her actions on Friday.
"She hasn't appropriated any motifs, or themes, or forms of Aboriginal art at all, and she hasn't appropriated the personality of any actual person," he said in a radio interview.
"She has created a character, just as a playwright or a poet or a novelist will create a character."
Smith said Durack's art style was "an Aboriginal adaptation of Western techniques, which I would call in general terms expressionist".
A senior curator at South Australian state's Flinders Art Museum, Doreen Mellor, demanded Durack apologise.
"As an Aboriginal person, I feel really offended, I feel very angry that these sorts of things can actually happen.
"Thousands of people have been very moved by the combination of Burrup's invented words, the photographs and the paintings."
